overview: Three despatches from American Consul Gerald Warner at Taihoku document a succession of destructive tropical storms affecting Japanese-ruled Taiwan and the Spratly Islands between August and December 1940. They describe the paths and wind speeds of the storms, damage to crops and infrastructure, flooding and loss of life, the sinking of the American yacht CYNJO at Keelung, and the devastation of the sparsely populated Spratly Islands by a typhoon and tidal wave. Together, the reports provide contemporary consular observations of disaster severity, economic losses, communications difficulties, and relief measures.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 117 on the typhoon of August 30, 1940
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the meteorological, agricultural, infrastructural, and maritime damage caused by the August 30 typhoon in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The Taihoku Weather Bureau characterized the storm as Taiwan's worst typhoon in nine years, with sustained winds around 25 meters per second and a record peak of 40 meters per second. It traveled up the eastern coast from Karenko through Keelung, damaging bananas, sugar cane, rice, cotton, tobacco, hemp, property, roads, and railways, although comparatively light rainfall limited flooding. The American yacht CYNJO, owned by Joseph C. Sever, sank at its Keelung moorings and was being raised for eventual shipment abroad.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 122 on the typhoon of September 29–30, 1940
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports extensive agricultural and property damage from Taiwan's third and worst typhoon of the 1940 season.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports that Taiwan's worst typhoon in 26 years struck on September 29 and continued through September 30, with its center over southern Taiwan and peak winds reportedly reaching 48 meters per second. Preliminary estimates suggested that wind and flooding destroyed 10–20 percent of agricultural crops, especially the approaching rice harvest and mature or newly planted sugar cane. The storm also caused considerable property destruction and some loss of life and was the third typhoon to affect Taiwan during the season.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 130 on the Shinnan Gunto typhoon and tidal wave
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the destruction and relief response following the December 5 typhoon and tidal wave in the Spratly Islands.
subfiles.summary: Local press reports stated that a typhoon and an 18-foot tidal wave swept over Shinnan Gunto on December 5, demolishing all buildings and leaving about eight people dead, several dozen wounded, and roughly forty missing. The disaster was especially severe because the islands were low-lying and supported only about 300 Japanese residents, mainly on Naga Shima. Destruction of communications delayed news reaching Takao for a week, after which four shiploads of medical supplies, food, and other relief goods were dispatched. Warner refers the Department to his May 9, 1939 despatch for a fuller description of the islands and their incorporation into Taiwan's jurisdiction.

interest: The file offers a compact sequence of reports on an unusually destructive 1940 typhoon season, allowing comparison of three storms across Taiwan and its recently acquired island dependencies. It is particularly useful for environmental and economic history because it records wind speeds, crop-specific losses, flood-control performance, transportation damage, casualties, communications delays, and emergency relief. The sinking of the American yacht CYNJO connects the natural-disaster reports to the experiences of foreign residents, while the Spratly Islands despatch provides evidence about Japanese settlement and administration of the disputed islands shortly before the Pacific War.
